n: The messenger continues from chapter 10, mentioning that he had strengthened Darius the Mede (or Michael) in that king’s first year. Behind earthly thrones, heavenly helpers are at work.

f.w: stood to confirm and to strengthen him
f.g: “Him” may be Darius or Michael (Daniel 10:21).

n: This chapter is the most detailed prophecy in the Old Testament. Three more Persian kings will come, then a fourth, very rich, who will provoke Greece. Many identify him with Xerxes I, who invaded Greece in 480 BC.

f.w: the fourth shall be far richer than they all
f.g: Commonly identified as Xerxes I (Ahasuerus of Esther).
Greece.

n: A mighty king will rise and do whatever he wants—Alexander the Great (336–323 BC).
At his height his empire breaks into four parts, not passed to his heirs. Alexander’s young sons were killed, and his generals divided the empire.

f.w: divided toward the four winds of heaven

n: From here on, “the king of the south” means Egypt’s Ptolemaic rulers and “the king of the north” the Seleucid rulers of Syria. Israel lay between them. Ptolemy I was strong, but one of his former officers, Seleucus I, grew even stronger.

f.g: The Ptolemies, Greek kings of Egypt.
Probably Seleucus I, once Ptolemy’s officer, who founded the northern (Seleucid) kingdom.

n: Years later, a peace treaty is sealed by marriage: Berenice, daughter of Ptolemy II, married the Seleucid king Antiochus II. The alliance failed—she, her child, and her attendants were murdered.

f.w: the king's daughter of the south
f.g: Berenice, married to Antiochus II about 252 BC.

f.w: she shall not retain the power of the arm
f.g: She will not keep her influence.

n: Her brother, “a branch from her roots”—Ptolemy III—avenged her by invading the northern kingdom and winning.

f.g: A relative—her brother Ptolemy III.
In his place, as successor.

n: He carried back to Egypt captured idols, officials, and treasures of silver and gold, and outlived the northern king.
The northern king (Seleucus II) tried a counterattack on Egypt but was forced to return home.
The northern king’s sons gathered great armies. One of them, Antiochus III (“the Great”), swept south like a flood toward Egypt’s fortress.

f.g: Sweep through like a flood.

n: The furious southern king (Ptolemy IV) fought back. At the battle of Raphia (217 BC) he defeated Antiochus III’s huge army.

f.g: Anger, rage.

n: Victory made the southern king proud, and he killed tens of thousands—but he did not follow up his advantage.
Years later the northern king returned with an even larger, richer army.
Many rose against the south, including some violent men among the Jews who tried to fulfill prophecy by force—but they failed.

f.g: Violent men among your own people.
Trying to bring a prophecy to pass by their own efforts.

n: The northern king besieged and took a fortified city—likely Sidon, after Antiochus III won the battle of Panium (about 200 BC). Egypt’s best troops couldn’t stop him.

f.g: Build a siege ramp.
A well-fortified city.

n: Now unopposed, he took control of “the glorious land”—Judea passed from Egyptian to Seleucid rule around 198 BC.

f.g: The beautiful land—Israel.

n: He tried to gain Egypt through marriage, giving his daughter (Cleopatra I) to young Ptolemy V. But she sided with her husband and Egypt rather than her father.

f.g: A young woman—his daughter Cleopatra I.

n: He turned to the coastlands of Asia Minor and Greece, but a commander—the Roman Lucius Scipio—stopped him at Magnesia (190 BC), turning his insolence back on him.

f.g: Coastlands—Asia Minor and the Greek islands.
Insolence, scorn.

n: He retreated to his own fortresses, then stumbled and fell. Antiochus III died in 187 BC while trying to plunder a temple in Elymais to pay his debts to Rome.
His successor (Seleucus IV) sent a tax collector—traditionally Heliodorus—to raise funds, even from the Jerusalem temple. He reigned briefly and was assassinated, not in battle.

f.g: One who sends out a tax collector.
Possibly the temple in Jerusalem, the kingdom’s glory.

n: Next comes a “contemptible person” who wasn’t the rightful heir but took the throne through intrigue and flattery: Antiochus IV Epiphanes (175–164 BC), the “little horn” of chapter 8.

f.g: A despicable man—Antiochus IV, who called himself Epiphanes (“God manifest”).

n: Opposing armies are swept away before him, and even “the prince of the covenant” is broken—probably the high priest Onias III, who was removed and later murdered.

f.g: Probably the high priest Onias III.

n: He makes alliances and then breaks them through deceit, rising to power with only a small following.

f.g: Alliance, treaty.

n: He invades rich provinces and lavishly distributes plunder to buy loyalty—something his predecessors hadn’t done. He plots against fortresses, but only for a time; God sets the limit.

f.g: Devise plans, plot.
Only for a limited time.

n: He launches a great army against Egypt (170–169 BC). The southern king (Ptolemy VI) fights back but is defeated, partly through plots against him.
Ptolemy’s own advisers—those who ate at his table—betray him, and his army is overwhelmed.

f.w: they that feed of the portion of his meat
f.g: Those who eat at his table—his trusted advisers.

n: The two kings sit at one table, lying to each other with evil intent, but neither succeeds—the outcome is in God’s hands at the appointed time.

f.w: they shall speak lies at one table
f.g: Antiochus IV and his nephew Ptolemy VI negotiated with mutual deceit.

n: Returning home rich, Antiochus turns against the holy covenant. In 169 BC he plundered the Jerusalem temple.

f.w: his heart shall be against the holy covenant
f.g: Hostile to the Jews’ religion and covenant with God.

n: He invades Egypt again (168 BC), but this time the outcome is different.

Ships from Kittim—Romans—confront him. A Roman envoy famously drew a circle in the sand and ordered him to decide before stepping out of it; humiliated, Antiochus withdrew and vented his rage on the Jews, favoring those who abandoned the covenant.

f.g: Kittim—originally Cyprus, later used for western powers such as Rome.

f.w: have intelligence with them that forsake the holy covenant
f.g: Show favor to Jews who abandoned their faith.

n: His forces desecrate the temple, stop the daily sacrifice, and set up “the abomination that makes desolate”—in 167 BC an altar to Zeus was placed on the temple altar. Jesus later spoke of a future “abomination of desolation.”

f.g: The temple fortress.

n: He seduces covenant-breakers with flattery, but those who know their God stand firm and act boldly—like the Maccabees who resisted. Knowing God gives strength.

f.w: the people that do know their God shall be strong

f.g: Act with courage and effect.

n: The wise among the people will teach many, yet some will suffer martyrdom—by sword, fire, captivity, and plunder.

f.g: The wise or insightful (Hebrew maskilim).

f.w: they shall fall by the sword

n: When they fall, they will receive a little help—perhaps the Maccabean revolt—while some join them insincerely.

f.g: Helped.

n: Some of the wise will die, but their trials will refine, purify, and make them white—until the appointed end. Suffering for faith can purify the faithful.

f.w: to try them, and to purge, and to make them white

n: The king exalts himself above every god and blasphemes the God of gods, prospering only until God’s wrath runs its course. Antiochus fits this description, and many readers also see a pattern of a future anti-God figure.

f.g: Astonishing blasphemies.

n: He disregards his ancestors’ gods and “the one desired by women” (perhaps a popular god such as Tammuz), placing himself above all.

f.g: Possibly a deity popular with women, such as Tammuz or Adonis.

n: Instead he honors a “god of fortresses”—military power—with lavish gifts. His true god is force.

f.g: A god of fortresses or military might.

n: With this foreign god’s help he attacks strongholds, rewards supporters with rule over many, and parcels out land for profit.

“At the time of the end,” the southern king attacks him, and the northern king storms back with chariots, cavalry, and ships. Many scholars note that verses 40–45 don’t match what is known of Antiochus IV’s last years; many interpreters apply them to the last days.

f.w: at the time of the end

n: He invades the glorious land and overthrows many countries, but Edom, Moab, and Ammon escape.

f.w: Edom, and Moab, and the chief of the children of Ammon
f.g: Old neighbors of Israel, east of the Jordan.

n: Egypt will not escape his grasp.
He seizes Egypt’s treasures, with Libya and Cush (Ethiopia) under his control.

f.g: Following him—in submission.

n: Alarming reports from the east and north drive him out in fury to destroy many.

f.g: News, reports.

n: He pitches his royal tents between the sea and the holy mountain—yet he comes to his end with no one to help him. However mighty the persecutor, his end is certain.

f.w: between the seas in the glorious holy mountain
f.g: Between the Mediterranean and Mount Zion.

f.w: he shall come to his end, and none shall help him
